articles.title: New Ape Escape Reportedly in Development at Sonic Mania Team
articles.summary: A new Ape Escape video game is reportedly in the works, helmed by the team that successfully rebooted a certain blue hedgehog with Sonic Mania.
articles.body:
A new Ape Escape video game is reportedly in the works, helmed by the team that successfully rebooted a certain blue hedgehog with Sonic Mania . Developer Evening Star also made Penny’s Big Breakaway , which launched to mixed reviews compared to Sonic Mania’s near unanimous praise.

The report comes from journalist Jeff Gerstmann, corroborated by VGC sources. “So yeah, some other folks have said that they also heard that Ape Escape is being made,” Gerstmann said on his podcast .

“I don’t think this game is close to being out or anything like that, but I guess it’s been almost a year since we started talking about Ape Escape. “Who is making it? That’s a good question.

The 100 Best PlayStation Games of All Time

“My understanding is that it’s an external studio. People were immediately like, ‘Oh, Team Asobi (Astro Bot) is making it.’ My understanding is that an external team has been working on that. What do they make… Penny’s Big Breakaway. Evening Star. I heard that they were working on it.”

According to the report, Sony is looking at using third-party studios to revive dormant series across its entire portfolio. Last month, rumors were circulating that PlayStation is looking to bring back Killzone , though the obvious choice of developer for that one would likely be first-party original studio Guerrilla Games.

The last game in the Ape Escape series is PlayStation Move Ape Escape, released for PS3 in 2010. The last mainline game was Ape Escape 3, five years earlier, for PS2.

“At the time that I initially heard it, it sounded like it was a game that had been just barely greenlit and just getting underway," Gerstmann continued.

“You know, not necessarily the most corroborated, multiple-source thing, but that is what I heard about an Ape Escape Game. I was asking people questions at DICE this year about this Ape Escape game. So that was February. So there ya go.”

IGN reached out to Sony for comment about its rumored third-party licensing strategy last week, but so far there’s been no response.

articles.title: Someone Used AI to Make Minecraft Playable Inside Twitter With Working Multiplayer, and Immediately Sold Sponsorships via Crypto
articles.summary: The AI video game clone explosion continues at pace. Now, someone has made Minecraft playable inside X / Twitter with working multiplayer.
articles.body:
The AI video game clone explosion continues at pace. Now, someone has made Minecraft playable inside X / Twitter with working multiplayer. X user jaivin used AI to make Mojang’s Minecraft playable inside posts on Elon Musk’s social network, and is letting people buy in-game sponsorships with cryptocurrency.

“Tweetcraft is a block game in a post: every world is a link on X, and everyone who opens it plays together,” reads the official blurb. “Put your ad at the top of the server list, in a world’s sponsor leaderboard, or your logo on the Block Dragon.”

So, what’s going on here? Essentially, "Tweetcraft" is a custom browser-based Minecraft clone where you generate a shared world and post its unique link on X / Twitter, which acts as a shared entry point. Anyone who clicks on the link joins the same real-time multiplayer session. The game itself renders in your browser.

This “port” is, obviously, unauthorized, and will no doubt draw the attention of Microsoft’s lawyers sooner rather than later. Jaivin’s launch post has had 7.4 million views already. Various follow-up posts detail an explosion of popularity as people try it out.

Perhaps in a bid to downplay any potential trademark or copyright infringement, jaivin has called the game “Tweetcraft,” although it’s clearly Minecraft in shape and form. Jaivin also insisted that “Tweetcraft uses none of Minecraft's assets and is not associated with Mojang or Microsoft.”

Responses are similar to those we’ve seen over the last two weeks amid this AI-powered video game clone and “game-merging” mod explosion, which has spawned a number of viral gameplay clips of famous video game franchises mashed together. There’s a mix of excitement and disgust, with some saying a clampdown is inevitable.

“The name is brilliant because now you can lose two separate trademark lawsuits,” one person said of Tweetcraft.

“The ‘I do not own this music video’ description when uploading a music video on YouTube defense,” another said.

Clearly, this Whack-a-Mole between IP owner and AI-generated video game isn’t sustainable, so the question will be what the video game industry does long term to prevent this sort of thing happening in the first place. Indeed, can it do anything? With AI models becoming increasingly powerful, the time it takes for unauthorized versions of established video games to appear outside of official platforms will reduce potentially to just hours or even minutes. With GTA 6 releasing on PS5 and Xbox Series X and S only, how long will it take for someone to use AI to make it playable on PC via a browser?

Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: Aaron Sorkin Takes on Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg Again With The Social Reckoning But With Mixed Results
articles.summary: Jeremy Strong is captivating as an almost alien-like incarnation of Mark Zuckerberg and a smart and sympathetic Mikey Madison shines as the whistleblower who outed Facebook’s corporate secrets. But filmmaker Aaron Sorkin’s work here proves a mixed bag, delivering a sharp script but bringing it to life with workman-like direction.
articles.body:
The Social Reckoning opens in theaters on October 9.

Aaron Sorkin, who won an Oscar for scripting The Social Network , returns to exploring the sins of Facebook with The Social Reckoning , a sequel companion piece to that David Fincher-directed 2010 film that feels late to its own party.

The Sorkin-directed film chronicles how Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) collaborated with Facebook data scientist Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) to reveal the social media company’s dirtiest laundry in the 2021 multi-article series The Facebook Files . Thanks to the information and documents that Frances leaked to Jeff, the Journal claimed to expose how the platforms owned by mogul Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong , stepping in for Jesse Eisenberg ) knowingly made life shittier for everybody so they could stay profitable. It’s more complex than that but that’s the gist.

Despite being sharply written and engagingly performed by a great cast, The Social Reckoning never reaches the dramatic heights of its 2010 predecessor. The Social Network was a more personal story about ambitious young friends dreaming big and ferociously falling out. It was a story where people confront each other face to face.

The Social Reckoning, on the other hand, is a whistleblower/journalist movie where the main conflict is between a hero who is only in the same room with the villain once and never speaks to them. Sorkin’s script is entertaining and features his signature punchy, smarmy dialogue that actors love to say, but many of these characters feel like functionaries.

We don't learn much about Jeff except that he’s ignorant about tech but is a good reporter. White is decent here but not particularly compelling. Madison’s nerdy Frances has more dimension, as her occasional mean streak helps mask her own social awkwardness. She’s a sympathetic protagonist even if her life beyond Facebook, like Jeff’s beyond the Journal, remains largely unknown. (The scene where she is on a date with a finance bro is pretty funny, though.)

On the Facebook side, Jeremy Strong isn’t in the film as much as you might expect, but he possesses the screen every moment he’s on it. He plays Zuckerberg as the creepiest android that Weyland-Yutani ever built, a humanoid construct missing some key components that prevent him from fully functioning. The film’s stellar ensemble also includes solid turns by Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Betty Gilpin, and Billy Magnussen.

As much as his dialogue can crackle, Sorkin the director struggles to make The Social Reckoning pop. The film plays like a stage production that was adapted for the screen but without capturing the electricity you’d have felt when it was on Broadway. It’s competently directed but rarely rousing. Even when the music is telling you to be roused.

Despite Alexandre Desplat’s melodramatic score pounding the viewer over the head to tell us how important Frances’ congressional testimony is — the film is well aware of its Frank Capra aspirations as the Mr. Smith Goes to Washington director gets name-checked in one amusing scene — we know we still live in a world where Facebook’s tactics were exposed and … life just went on.

It’s depressing, I know, but that’s the sad truth. Even Zuckerberg’s tenure as the face of tech villainy has mostly waned with Sam Altman and Elon Musk — both of whom also have movies about them coming out soon — now dominating the cultural conversation.

In some ways, it’s not the film’s fault that the outrage it’s asking the viewer to feel lacks urgency. We live in a time where there’s at least one or two news stories every day that spark outrage. It’s exhausting, so asking the viewer to reconnect with issues that polarized people five to seven years ago — the film brings us back to the glory days of the COVID-19 pandemic and the January 6th insurrection — is a lot, especially when its ultimate message isn’t exactly new or shocking: Social media, specifically Facebook, is a monster that divides people, makes life worse, spreads misinformation and earns a pretty penny off all of that misery.

articles.title: Review: Samuel L. Jackson’s President Strikes Back With Great Vengeance and Furious Anger in Renny Harlin's The Beast
articles.summary: Samuel L. Jackson brings a mix of badassery and vulnerability to the role of President of the United States in The Beast, director Renny Harlin's a fun throwback to high-concept action movies of the past.
articles.body:
The Beast will be released in theaters on October 9.

Samuel L. Jackson reunites with his The Long Kiss Goodnight and Deep Blue Sea director Renny Harlin for The Beast , a fun, exciting throwback to the high-concept action-thrillers of yesteryear. The film’s premise is simple but never dull: The President of the United States (Jackson) finds himself trapped inside his own armored fortress of a limousine (The Beast of the title) after terrorists attack him and wipe out nearly his entire Secret Service detail.

POTUS must drive himself and his wounded Secret Service agent, Taft (Joel Kinnaman), through a war zone to reach the designated extraction point. Unfortunately, getting there is nearly impossible as some unidentified alliance of enemies has launched a simultaneous attack on the U.S. and multiple other nations, developments that have abruptly left the whole world in upheaval.

The enemy’s agenda is murky but their firepower and expertise has essentially crippled the entire U.S. national defense apparatus. Thankfully for POTUS, The Beast isn’t just an armored car; it also has plenty of hi-tech offensive weapons to fight back with. It’s basically The President’s Batmobile.

Relentlessly paced, The Beast plays out in real time. The movie literally starts with a bang – watch the opening three minutes here – and never lets up. Terms like “full throttle” and “high-octane” are bandied about in movie marketing all the time, but The Beast is one of the few movies that can sincerely sell itself that way.

The Beast is basically a two-hander on wheels, as Jackson and Kinnaman share the screen together almost the entire time. Taft is bleeding out in the backseat like Mr. Orange in Reservoir Dogs, but POTUS refuses to put himself first despite protocol. POTUS uses everything at his disposal inside The Beast to ward off the unending droves of attackers, while also trying to keep Taft awake and alive. Jackson and Kinnaman have good chemistry together but, as should be expected, no one can act Sam Jackson off the screen. Jackson holds the viewer’s attention the whole time.

Jackson’s POTUS is a Vietnam War veteran whose PTSD is retriggered by the attack and all the bloodshed that ensues. He’s wracked with survivor’s guilt from the war and from all the people who are dying for him now. He thought his inner demons were under control thanks to the help of his wife Rosa (voiced by Jackson’s real wife, actress LaTanya Richardson Jackson). (The First Lady, mind you, is also in peril on the other side of town.) All of which is to say the terrorists just pissed off the wrong President because this guy was trained to kill. Hail to the muthafuckin’ Chief!

The Beast’s race through the now war-ravaged streets of L.A. plays like that final convoy run in Black Hawk Down but within the lawlessness of The Purge or Grand Theft Auto. This is a behind enemy lines film but where the lines have been drawn on what had once been your own safe soil. Harlin and screenwriter Umair Aleem conjure old-school John Carpenter (Assault on Precinct 13) and Walter Hill (The Warriors) vibes, forging The Beast into a lean, mean B-movie that certainly deserves consideration the next time there are lists written about “one crazy night” movies or films that all take place within one location. (Even the score by Tuomas Kantelinen has a John Carpenter/Escape from New York synth sound to it.)

Harlin shot the limo scenes on an LED stage (similar to how Matt Reeves’ shot Robert Pattinson and Colin Farrell in the Batmobile vs. Penguin chase sequence from The Batman) so Jackson and Kinnaman could see all the mayhem rather than just imagine it. There are 360-degree shots inside The Beast, but it’s not overused and helps orient the viewer and understand the geography of the car and what it holds.

The Beast may not break any new ground in the action-thriller genre, but it does claw back those fundamental elements that led filmgoers to enjoy it to begin with.

articles.title: Forza Horizon 6 Reportedly Coming to PS5 in January on Disc
articles.summary: According to a report from French site Dealabs, Forza Horizon 6 will finally land on PS5 early next year.
articles.body:
According to a report from reliable leaker billbil-kun on French site Dealabs , Forza Horizon 6 will finally land on PS5 early next year, despite Microsoft insisting it would make it out by the end of 2026.

Playground's well-received racer launched on Xbox Series X and S and PC in May 2026. The PS5 version is now set to dodge a collision with GTA 6 , which seems to have its own track and street racing, and will reportedly release on January 26, 2027.

In August, Tom Warren from The Verge said that Forza Horizon 6 wouldn't hit PS5 this year. At the time, Playground released a statement insisting Forza Horizon 6 would. Playground has yet to issue a fresh comment following today's report.

Since Xbox CEO Asha Sharma took over from the retired Phil Spencer earlier this year, Microsoft's gaming strategy has shifted to encompass limited Xbox console exclusives. Gears of War: E-Day, for example, will not release on PS5. Neither will inXile's Clockwork Revolution, which was made an Xbox console exclusive .

Forza Horizon 6, however, has avoided a similar fate. Perhaps that's no surprise, given Forza Horizon 5 reportedly sold over 5 million copies on PS5, generating more than $300 million in revenue. Surely Forza Horizon 6 will generate signifcant revenue on PS5 also.

IGN’s Forza Horizon 6 review returned a 10/10. We called it “the best-looking and best-sounding game Playground has produced to date, set in the most wonderfully realised map it’s ever crafted.”

According to billbil-kun, a PS5 physical edition will land at the same time as the digital version. Earlier this year, Sony announced plans to phase out discs on PlayStation by 2028 , sparking massive pushback and petitions with hundreds of thousands of signatories .

The report claims the price for Forza Horizon 6 on PS5 will align with the Xbox version, meaning it’ll cost around $69.99. As a first-party game, it's also available as part of Game Pass, although there are question marks over Microsoft's subscription strategy and day one releases . In July, the former director of Forza Horizon traced a line from the failure of the "well-meaning" Game Pass to the current layoffs sweeping across Xbox .

Just this week, Playground issued a statement finally addressing its community after months of constructive feedback about Forza Horizon 6 was met with nothing but radio silence from the renowned British studio. A second team at Playground is also in the final stretch of development on the Fable reboot, which is due to be released on Xbox, PC, and PS5 on February 23, 2027.

articles.title: ‘Why Hasn’t Someone Thought About That Before?’ – How Star Wars: Galactic Racer Solves One of Driving Games’ Biggest Problems
articles.summary: Racing games have been stuck using the same career mode formula since the original Gran Turismo, but Star Wars: Galactic Racer shows there's a better, more dangerous way.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Phil Iwaniuk, decorated winner of many Gran Turismo Sunday Cups who learned to feel, not think in 1999's Star Wars: Episode 1 Racer. It's a philosophy that may impair his opinions, but yields many a purple sector.

How many times have you bought a cheap banger, entered it in a series of races called something like the ‘Rookies Cup’, and used the proceeds to unlock new events? Since Gran Turismo arrived in 1997 and pioneered that vehicular rags-to-riches structure, it feels like we’ve repeated that identical racing game campaign mode grind countless times.

In fact, when you pause and look back at the great and good of racing games, it seems like all of them, from Need For Speed to Dirt Rally, were about putting you at the bottom of a big pile of events and having you gradually climb your way up to the faster races in the best cars. The genre’s been laser-focussed on innovating when it comes to visuals, physics models, tire simulation and the like, but it’s been stuck on the same solo gameplay structure for way too long.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer flies its speeders against the grain in many ways. More than just a game that gets both the cinematic IP and the feeling of racing right, it’s an experience that seems to be visiting from a parallel universe. One where the familiar hand-holding game design philosophy didn’t take root, and the Gran Turismo career mode didn’t become ubiquitous.

“Why hasn’t someone thought about that before?” Fuse Games co-founder and CEO, Matt Webster, reflected on the game’s unique run-based career mode when IGN spoke to him back in May. It’s so obvious that it would make for a fantastic racer when you see it implemented like this: instead of working through a to-do list of championships, you pick from a selection of different sequences of events, each with their own risks and rewards, and if you lose too many times along the way you’re booted out of the whole championship. It’s back to the start for you, and no excuses. Even before you get familiar with the nuances of the mode, there’s something about knowing losing actually matters that feels refreshing.

“Gaming is risk-reward”, says Webster, “but the risk has to have a consequence.” In Webster’s previous racing hits like Burnout, that consequence looked like a spectacular wreck, your car resetting on the track, and you having some catching up to do.

“But we've lost consequence because, in many racing games, we don't really spend the time on crashing,” he adds. “It’s been eroded away. So [we] looked at different genres that you could steal from, because genres have done that in contemporary gaming. We see lots of hybrid mechanics going in, and actually racing is a bit of an outlier that hasn't done that.”

Instead, racing has gone in one of two directions recently. The post-covid sim racing boom seemed to convince developers of the more hardcore titles that the PvP-focused iRacing model is king. Why spend such a lot of effort on a career mode built around PvE racing when your player base is queuing up in lobbies, waiting to provide more intelligent and unpredictable competition than even the smartest AI drivers? The success of Assetto Corsa Competizione and Le Mans Ultimate has only strengthened that argument.

At the other end of the spectrum lies the Forza Horizon model. Friendly, malleable, and totally player-directed, its structure is basically failure-proof. Forza Horizon 6 set a new standard for open-world racing in 2026, capturing the crystallised essence of Japanese car culture and giving you many ways to explore them. But does losing a race really carry much weight at the Horizon festival?

Like an encouraging parent, Horizon treats everything you do as a victory. Oh, you drove through another mascot, great job! it cooes. Wow, and that’s 25% of all the roads explored now – someone deserves a cheeky wheelspin . So when you do actually take on something difficult and prevail, the payoff is dulled not because the game doesn’t recognise it, but because it treats you like its favourite special little driver, no matter whether you win or lose.

So yes, it feels like an oddly radical move that Star Wars: Galactic Racer implements a narrative-led championship mode and gives you real consequences for wrecking your vehicle and losing races. But it goes so much further than that. Turning career mode into a series of runs makes it a playground for experimenting with different builds in, and that’s something racing games just don’t do.

Along each run in Galactic Racer you earn credits, parts, abilities, and upgrades. Some of those rewards are pretty orthodox and can be used for straightforward buffs like a better cornering stat or a higher top speed, as we’ve been accustomed to in the genre for decades.

But many rewards come with an RNG-ified twist. Say during one run, you see an upgrade card that makes your ramjet booster 20% more powerful while you’re overheated. You remember that the next planet you’re racing on is Jakku, a scorched desert where your speeder overheats almost instantly. So you start to design your whole build around overheating quickly and staying overheated, to give your ram jet godlike power. Get it wrong and you blow up, incurring damage that must be repaired so that it doesn’t impair your stats and abilities. Get it right, and you feel like you’re on that unstoppable Balatro run.

Better still, the run structure has a way of turning all the game’s other brilliant little flourishes into important roguelite variables. Most obvious are the status effects you’ll encounter on each planet’s widely differing climate and conditions. The aforementioned Jakku brings the risk of overheating, while Ando Prime presents the opposite problem: its glacial plains will freeze your engines unless you find warmer pockets. Your interplanetary championship hop might include several status effects to be wary of.

On its own, this addition gets you thinking about taking different lines through tracks, to find shade on hot planets or look for ramps over corrosive pools. And that’s great in itself, but when combined with the parts and upgrades available in each run, it becomes the inspiration for specific vehicle builds. You can turn ostensibly negative status effects to your advantage.

And it goes deeper. Little touches like the pre-race checks – essentially QTEs that make you feel like you’re arming various aspects of your vehicle – on their own are just a nice touch that makes you feel somehow more physically in control and planted in your vehicle. But as you go through a run, you pick up backers who fund your racing and provide tokens. On one run, a particular backer might reward you for completing a certain number of pre-race checks, and you might really need those reward credits to repair your ramjet. Suddenly a nice touch becomes an important part of the story of this run.

The potential for that structure to shake up other racing games is just so juicy. EA F1’s driver career mode is no slouch, but imagine how it’d be elevated if, when you crashed your car, it gave you real and lasting consequences to deal with. What if being busted by the cops in Need For Speed didn’t just lose you credits, but your car and your career mode progress too?

Hardcore racing simulators shouldn’t turn a blind eye, either. If you’re willing to brave unranked public lobbies and scrutinise toe-in angles, it’s not a leap to imagine that a solo career where failure carries consequences might appeal.

Maybe it’s the open world racing game that can crib most effectively from Star Wars: Galactic Racer, though. Forza Horizon 6’s no-fail, maximalist approach is tremendous fun, but the sense of progress and accomplishment is hurt by the pace it throws cars and credits at you, win or lose. What if each entry to Horizon Festival told a different story, and making it onto Legend Island wasn’t a given?

“In an open world racer, you can decide [what] you're going to get after” says Fuse creative director Kieran Crimmins. “You can essentially do everything. Whereas in this, you've got to make the choice. Those choices really matter and they may be your ultimate demise or the path to victory.”

Like Half-Life’s Gravity Gun, the Crysis Nanosuit, and Shadow of Mordor’s (egregiously copyrighted) Nemesis System, what Fuse Games has created here is the sort of system you actively miss in other games. The sort of idea that could level up a genre if it proliferates. And there’s signs that it will. Galactic Racer is not the only roguelite motorsport game to have launched this year – we’ve also seen Carmageddon: Rogue Shift and Driving Rogue, both of which were developed in parallel with Fuse’s work. Clearly it’s not just Webster and his team that have recognised how this formula can be fitted into the genre’s engine bay. At long last, racing games have found a way to tell emergent stories and to reward replayability with build experimentation, and that finally lets go of the Rookies Cup.

Phil Iwaniuk is a veteran hardware smasher and game botherer who has written for the likes of PC Format, Official PlayStation Magazine, PCGamesN, The Guardian, Eurogamer, Rock, Paper, Shotgun, and IGN. He won an award once, but he doesn't like to go on about it.

articles.title: Mafia 2 and Mafia 3 Could Be Set for PS5 and Xbox Series Upgrades After Definitive Editions Leak Online
articles.summary: Mafia 2 and Mafia 3 are coming to PS5 and Xbox Series consoles with some prettier graphics, according to an ESRB rating.
articles.body:
Mafia 2 and Mafia 3 are coming to PS5 and Xbox Series consoles with some prettier graphics, according to an ESRB rating. Both games are rated Mature 17+ by the board, with each title featuring violence, nudity, and so… many… slurs.

Previously, Mafia: Definitive Edition released for modern consoles in September 2020. A full-blown, ground-up remake of the original 2002 game, it acted as a great starting point for people jumping into the series for the first time. Mafia 2 and 3 Definitive Editions already exist for the last-gen consoles, so these listings presumably relate to current-gen upgrades that will, hopefully, include 60fps gameplay, rather than full-blown remakes.

Publisher 2K recently released the Mafia: The Omertà Collection, which includes all the Definitive Editions alongside Mafia: The Old Country Definitive Edition. This launched alongside a PS5 and Xbox Series update to Mafia: Definitive Edition that seems likely to be replicated for Mafia 2 and 3.

Interest in the series is at a new high following the release of Mafia: The Old Country earlier this year. A prequel story set at the height of the mob’s power in Italy, it followed the series’ template of plonking players into an open world that serves as a backdrop to the story, rather than a character in it.

IGN’s Mafia: The Old Country review scored it an 8/10, and called the game an “effective return to the linear and tightly story-driven format of the original Mafia and Mafia 2.” Mafia 3 split critics at launch because it leaned into its open world and made players complete repeatable missions to capture territory and progress the story. Amazing soundtrack, though.

Hangar 13 president Nick Baynes previously told IGN that Mafia and GTA — despite sharing a parent company — exist in two separate camps. “I think that genuinely at the studio, we've got our own path,” Baynes said. “It genuinely never ever comes up in conversation as a touchpoint or steering our strategy or anything like that.”

The ESRB posting doesn’t give much away, besides rehashing themes you’d expect from a game series named after an organized crime group. It’ll be interesting to see which side of GTA 6 ’s release date this November these Definitive Editions end up. Because while the games are fairly different, the audience only has limited disposable income and that choice has probably already been made if the games land anywhere near each other.

IGN just put out a big GTA 6 interview with Rockstar North studio head Rob Nelson , in which we spoke to him as he played a section of the game in front of us. Nelson spoke about its approach to open world design, and creating a game where “just existing” is a viable playstyle, living in Vice City and playing it almost like a life simulator.

It’s a very different approach to Mafia, in which the open world is simply a backdrop to the story. Still, isn’t it great that we live in a world where both approaches are viable and we get to experience it all?

A Mafia 2 and Mafia 3: Definitive Edition announcement is likely imminent, either way. My best guess would be The Game Awards this December, with a launch early next year. While you wait to find out, check out IGN's in-depth feature, 25 Years of Mafia Video Games: An Oral History .

articles.title: Gears of War: E-Day Studio Boss Insists 'The Next Game Will Not Take Nearly as Long' to Make, Responds to Layoff Concern
articles.summary: The boss of Gears of War: E-Day developer The Coalition has responded to reports that staff at the studio are worried they will lose their jobs amid the ongoing cuts at Xbox, and promised the next Gears game won’t take as long to make.
articles.body:
The boss of Gears of War: E-Day developer The Coalition has responded to reports that staff at the studio are worried they will lose their jobs amid the ongoing cuts at Xbox, and promised the next Gears game won’t take as long to make.

Earlier this month, Eurogamer reported on serious internal concern that layoffs would hit The Coalition after the release of E-Day. "The mood is certainly 'let's not celebrate the game until we're three months post launch, just in case,' which is very unusual," one source told the site. "We're just expecting the next wave [of layoffs], or being reorganized under Activision or something later this year," claimed another.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma’s “reset” of Microsoft’s gaming business has seen nearly 2,000 people cut already this financial year, with more to come. A number of studios have left the business or are in the process of closing down. Microsoft has also reorganized its studios, bringing Halo and Sea of Thieves developer Rare under Call of Duty developer Activision, and Grounded developer Obsidian under Fallout developer Bethesda.

The Coalition has, for the most part, avoided the cuts, although E-Day's story director was laid off just one week before the game's early access launch . The BBC put Eurogamer’s report to The Coalition studio head Mike Crump, who danced around the issue in his response.

"What I say to myself, what I say to the team, is we need to focus on the things that we can control,” Crump said.

"For us that's about shipping a great game that people are going to love and I feel like, as a team, we've done that."

No guarantee, then, that The Coalition will escape the fate suffered by so many at Xbox this summer. But Crump did suggest there are plans for more Gears of War games. He called E-Day a "great foundation" for future games in the series, and said "the next game will not take nearly as long" to make.

As for what the next Gears game is, in June 2024, Microsoft pledged to continue the story of Gears of War and wrap up the cliffhanger posed by Gears 5's ending, despite creating a prequel first with E-Day. The question is, will The Coalition get the chance to make it?

articles.title: The Odyssey Returns to IMAX as Digger's Run Comes to an End a Week After Launch
articles.summary: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is set to return to IMAX as Digger's run comes to an end a week after launch.
articles.body:
Tom Cruise’s latest movie, Digger, made around $20 million worldwide on its opening weekend. The film, which buries Cruise under thick makeup to make the ageless star look like a normal old man, reportedly had a $160 million production budget (via Deadline ). I’m no math genius, but is that good?

Meanwhile, Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey currently sits at $1.76 billion from theatres after what has been a spectacular run at the box office. Again, I’m not a math guy, but that’s a fair bit more.

Digger , which was shot in VistaVision, was released on IMAX screens on October 2, but its time on the bigger big screen is almost at an end already. The Odyssey will return to select IMAX theaters this Friday, October 9, replacing the Cruise flick.

The Odyssey Cast and Characters: Who's Who in the Christopher Nolan Film

With only 41 theatres worldwide equipped to play true IMAX, fitted with the specialized 15-perf/70mm film projectors capable of displaying the movie in its ideal ratio, it’s understandable. Especially if those cinemas want to make any money.

The next films with planned IMAX releases are Street Fighter on October 16, and Godzilla Minus Zero starting on November 3. Until then, there’s a small window of opportunity to see The Odyssey as Nolan intended.

IGN’s review of Digger called the script its "Achilles heel.” It has a 51% rating on Rotten Tomatoes' Tomatometer . Digger trolled the negative reviews in its most recent ad campaign, but that failed to move the needle.

The Odyssey was, of course, well-received, but it didn’t please everyone. Emily Wilson, the translator whose work inspired Nolan's adaptation of Homer's poem, hated it so much that she’s retranslating The Iliad in its entirety.

The Odyssey is currently the second highest-grossing movie of the year, behind only Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which has now passed well over $2 billion at the box office.

This headphone retails for $180 new and all other colorways are currently on sale for $130 so stick with rose gold for the biggest savings.

Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 Sport Headphones for $109.95

Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 Open-Ear Wireless Bone Conduction Sport Headphones

The OpenRun Pro 2 looks like a neckband style headphone except that the lightweight titanium band connecting the two ear pieces wraps around the back of your head instead of resting on your neck. This design does an excellent job of keeping everything in place, which is important because these are designed to be used while you're actively exercising.

Instead of the traditional method of sending sound vibrations to your eardrums, the OpenRun Pro uses bone conduction technology to send vibrations through your cheekbones directly to your inner ear. As such, the headphones are actually placed in front of your ear instead of on your ear. The biggest advantage is that you can fully hear your surroundings; if you like running on streets, for example, you'll be aware of everything that's going on around you while your music is playing.

OpenRun Pro 2 is an obvious upgrade over the Open Run Pro

The OpenRun Pro 2 is a substantial update over its predecessor. Probably the most noticeable upgrade is the switch from a proprietary magnetic charging cable to the USB Type-C standard. Another significant upgrade is the sound quality. While the original OpenRun Pro has good bass response, it is slightly hampered by the fact that it produces tiny vibrations that are noticeable and sometimes ticklish or distracting. The new OpenRun Pro 2 utilizes Shok's DualPitch technology to virtually eliminate vibrations. Other smaller changes include increased battery life and improved mic quality.

The Shokz OpenRun is the best earbuds for exercise

I have a pair of AirPods Pro that I use regularly, but I always set them aside for the OpenRun Pros when I run. The Transparency mode on the AirPods Pro does work well for most situations, but they still can't compare to the awareness you get without having any buds plugging up your ears. articles.title: A free mod for Titanfall 2 makes it one of the best VR games ever
articles.summary: Titanfall 2 VR is a mod created by a single developer, Jordan “CircuitLord” Juarez, that lets you play the whole campaign in a VR headset.
articles.body: Titanfall has a special place in my heart. I’ve never felt such a rush in gaming since — leaping into the air with a jump pack, running on walls, summoning a giant mechanized battle suit that falls like a meteor from the sky, then letting one of its giant hands stuff me into the cockpit for a supersized skirmish. How could that possibly work in virtual reality? It sounds like a formula for pain, nausea, distress. But no: Titanfall 2 VR is one of the top five VR games I’ve ever played — despite being a free mod, released by a solo developer, who’s only spent a single month working on it so far. Now I’m running on walls, blasting bad guys from every angle, shouldering a scoped anti-materiel sniper rifle nearly as big as Cloud Strife’s infamous Buster Sword, all in virtual reality — and, yes, leaping into a hulking Titan to dish out damage while snatching enemy missiles out of the air. [Media: I can look around the cockpit and move the Titan’s giant arms realistically with my own two hands. I can look down and watch my feet do the wall-running. A few hours in, I only feel the familiar twinge of simulator sickness if I shove the analog stick too far and turn my Titan too fast. The entire experience immediately brought me back to Capcom’s Resident Evil 4 VR, one of the only other full-length classic AAA games that has ever been remade for virtual reality and a completely comfortable experience for me. Why have so few decade-old games been given this treatment? Why aren’t dedicated VR games this good? That’s what Jordan “CircuitLord” Juarez would like to know, too. “VR has sort of been stuck, where developers and studios can’t commit to larger Triple A style games because they’re WAY harder to make for VR and the playerbase is so small, but the playerbase is so small because there’s no large or Triple A games being made,” the mod’s developer tells The Verge. “I think mods like this are a great way to jumpstart and hopefully break that loop to show studios how much fun VR really can be.” [Image: In his Discord channel, Juarez is somewhat less diplomatic about his reasoning, saying things to his fans like: * “A large reason I made this mod is out of spite because most VR developers have completely lost the plot” * “The only VR games I’d recommend to any adults are literally like 5+ years old” * “I’m here to make games I want to play, not slop geared towards kids” Juarez isn’t just a disgruntled VR fan — he’s a developer who had a front-row seat to the trend of kids becoming the primary customer for VR games. He says he worked on Gorilla Tag, the poster child for kids messing around in VR, as well as Zenith: The Last City, Synth Riders, and the 2020 Virtual Desktop competitor Desktop Portal. He also watched Meta inexplicably shut down one of his favorite games, Echo Arena, and he quit his job at VR studio Another Axiom after its Echo spiritual successor Orion Drift didn’t turn into the game he’d hoped for. This year, he started his own solo studio, Iteration Three, to build his own Echo Arena successor, No Shot. This fall, he decided to try a side project: Could he make existing games more playable in VR? In August, he revealed a VR mod for the popular Big Walk. In September, he announced he would do Titanfall 2 if he could manage to make it feel like “a true native VR experience, without any jank.” [Image: “I played Titanfall 2 years and years ago when it came out originally, always was a huge fan of it,” he tells me, and says a lot of the work was building custom interactions and reload animations, in addition to the obvious stuff like giving you a stereo 3D perspective and adding VR hands: > A specific example: the manual reloading for guns. The process involved basically splitting apart the existing animations and sound effects in the game, and hooking them up to VR related triggers instead. When you grab the magazine from over your shoulder, it positions it in your palm and plays a given animation on that hand to make it look like it’s grasping it. The gun itself has custom hitboxes I’ve set up for grabbing different parts of it, for example where you grab to rack the slide. This all took a TON of iteration given the large amount of guns in the game. He says he’s most proud of some special interactive moments he added that were previously cutscenes, like this one (warning, spoilers!): [Image: But, he tells me, Titanfall 2’s developers deserve the credit. “A lot of the praise I’m getting really should be going to the developers who crafted the amazing environments, sound effects, and story that so many people are now experiencing for the first time.” He’s also standing on the shoulders of Titanfall 2 community mod loader Northstar, which he uses to help integrate the mod. And yes, he did take advantage of AI too. While “basically all the game design stuff is still down to me,” he says, “AI has been really helpful on the reverse engineering side of things and for speeding up the development process in general.” [Image: One weird part: Most cutscenes play out on a flat screen instead of in immersive virtual reality. You can experimentally try VR there, but it’s jarring. Juarez’s work on Titanfall isn’t done: He says he’s getting a ton of requests to add multiplayer modes with private VR servers and is currently working on that. He’s also still patching the single-player campaign, which isn’t yet a perfect experience; occasionally I’ll try to look through a scope that’ll display as black rather than see-through, and I’ve had a few issues trying to pick up certain difficult-to-reach weapons. He recently tweaked it so Titans will turn when you aim your weapon far enough to the right or left, instead of just with a joystick. [Image: If you’ve got a PC and headset and want to try it for yourself, it shouldn’t be hard. Titanfall 2 is currently (and frequently) on sale for just $5, and the campaign is already quite playable on relatively modest PC hardware. Some say they’ve gotten it to run with an Nvidia GTX 1080 or a modern midrange RTX 3060 laptop GPU, since Titanfall 2 was always a very well-optimized PC game. You also don’t have to jump through many hoops to install it. The mod works with all three PC versions of Titanfall 2 and does practically everything in three clicks, though you do need to sign into the EA app and make sure SteamVR is running before you put your headset on. When I put on Meta’s VR Glasses, and when I reviewed the Steam Frame, I couldn’t help thinking: I wish we’d had this awesome new hardware before companies stopped investing in VR games! But now that we live in the recomp revolution, when pissed-off gamers and laid-off developers are channeling that energy (and a lot of AI) into breaking games free of their shackles, I wonder if this is the future of VR. Labors of love, and spite, standing atop the shoulders of those who came before.

OLED TVs are considered the best TVs for gaming . They're usually quite expensive, but Amazon is offering a fantastic deal on a Roku branded OLED TV during the October Prime Day Sale . For two days only, the 65" Roku Pro 4K OLED TV is available for $799.99 with free shipping. Alternatively, the 55" model is $699.99.

65" Roku 4K OLED TV for $799.99, 55" for $699.99

The Roku Pro-series OLED TV was released . It's equipped with a 4K true W-OLED panel with a native 120Hz refresh rate and HDMI 2.1 inputs, making it an excellent TV for PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X console gaming. Although the Roku Pro isn't as expensive as other OLED TVs, it shares most of the advantages of its more expensive siblings, including the near instaneous response time, true black levels, near infinite contrast ratio, and ultra-wide viewing angles. It also has one nice feature that the rest don't have, and that's the Roku smart interface baked in.

Roku is the best built-in smart interface

I've tried every built-in smart interface extensively, and I consider Roku to be the best smart interface overall compared to other popular options like Google TV (Sony), Tizen (Samsung), WebOS (LG), or Fire TV (Panasonic). Despite being a current generation console, the Nintendo Switch 2 has lax TV requirements compared to the PS5 or Xbox Series X. It can go up to 120fps if the resolution drops to 1080p, but the data rate required for both these options is pretty much the same, and you would much rather play any game in 4K. articles.title: Yankees’ season riding on one key piece — and it’s missing | Klapisch
articles.summary: The Bombers are turning to Max Fried to save them from elimination in the Division Series.
articles.body:
NEW YORK — It was October 2004, and if you're any kind of Yankees historian, you can probably guess where this analogy is headed.

It was Game 7 of the AL Championship Series when the Red Sox were about to put the finishing touches on a historic comeback against the Yankees. The Yankees had led the series 3-0, but now it was tied 3-3. Even though the Yankees had blown a three-game advantage, at least the deciding game was on their home turf.

The old Yankee Stadium was an uncomfortable place for visiting teams. The crowds were tougher back then, and the upper deck was massive, hanging low enough to intimidate outfielders.

The Red Sox had all the momentum. But the Yankees had the confidence that if all else failed, Yankee Stadium, the hard-edged fans and the remnants of the 1996-2000 dynasty would act as a last line of defense.

That narrative vanished in the space of one at-bat.

Johnny Damon led off the game with a sharp ground ball to third. The ball was hit one step to Alex Rodriguez's left — and he froze. He was tight. All the Yankees were.

Damon's base hit started a deluge that resulted in a 6-0 lead in the first two innings. The comeback was complete. So was the Yankees' humiliation.

Rodriguez wasn't solely responsible for the Yankees' 10-2 Game 7 loss, but the play confirmed my hunch they'd been traumatized by Boston's refusal to concede. The Yankees were beaten before they'd even stepped on the field.

I recalled that moment on Monday night at Tropicana Field, when I watched a similar scenario unfold in the best-of-five American League Division Series against the Rays: The Yankees were in a must-win situation — down 1-0 in the series — against an opponent with growing confidence. And then it happened.

Yandy Diaz led off the bottom of the first with a ground ball to the left of third baseman Ryan McMahon. It should've been an easy out, but McMahon allowed the ball to glance off his glove.

The error mushroomed into a catastrophic first inning for the Yankees, who made three errors. Even though Tampa Bay scored just one run, it was obvious which team had the upper hand.

Again, McMahon wasn't to blame for the eventual 5-2 loss. But it was an early indicator of the Yankees' lack of preparation. Starting pitcher Cam Schlittler bluntly said, "We didn't show up."

The question is whether the Yankees are capable of complete amnesia. They'll need it. Division Series history alone is daunting. Nearly 90% of teams that were down 0-2 in this best-of-five situation have gone on to lose.

For Wednesday's ALDS Game 3 between the Yankees and the Rays, the over/under is currently set at 7.5 total runs on Polymarket . Also, view our guide to the best sportsbook promos to shop for the odds across platforms.

Confidence matters as much as the numbers. The Rays have it — they are not afraid of the Yankees. The Yankees pretend to be unbothered, but I didn't sense much confidence in the post-game clubhouse.

That's because the Yankees had reason to expect dominance from Schlittler, similar to his masterpiece against Boston in the Wild Card Series.

The Red Sox were ready, or so they thought. They'd spent hours standing in against the hi-tech Trajekt machine. Boston's hitters memorized every trait of Schlittler's fastball, and he still shut them out over 6 1/3 innings in Game 1, striking out 10.

Schlittler encountered a much different opponent one week later. Unlike the Red Sox, the Rays don't strike out very often. They wear down even the hardest throwers, like Schlittler, by one foul ball after another.

The biggest shock to the Yankees was that Tampa Bay neutralized Schlittler's strikeout ability. He generated only two whiffs in 4 1/3 innings, leaving the Yankees in search of someone (anyone) who can help them regain their swagger.

Max Fried could be that guy, although not in the way Schlittler does. The left-hander prefers soft contact over swings and misses. Fried will need defensive support, and manager Aaron Boone must find new pieces around him

McMahon, for one, has to be replaced by Jose Caballero. That also goes for Jazz Chisholm; he needs to sit. Anthony Volpe is the most logical Plan B at second base.

But the Yankees will still need more than a new-look lineup to claw their way back into the series. They need to believe they can actually hang with the Rays. Their belief in their own superiority no longer sounds credible — not after a four-error fiasco and not after scoring two runs in 18 innings in the series.

Aaron Judge's absence has also destabilized the Yankees in ways that go beyond the box score. He's the Yankees' true leader. It doesn't matter if Judge is hitting home runs or mired in a slump. He's capable of lifting up the Yankees – but only when he's in the lineup. Seeing No. 99 in a hoodie in the dugout has, however subliminally, contributed to the Yankees' feeling of being underdogs.

It doesn't help, either, that Boone is not a war-time manager. He does his best work when the Yankees are cruising. Boone has the ability to keep all 26 players pulling in the same direction. He's an affirmer. He's all about positive energy.

What Boone lacks is the extra layer in his personality that demands more. He doesn't push the Yankees because he's not wired for that tension.

Can all this be fixed in one night? Pay attention to the first inning. It could be the key.

articles.title: Why Joe Davis is still sidelined for Dodgers-Braves NLDS series and who is replacing him
articles.summary: Braves fans will recognize the voice taking over for Davis in Wednesday's Game 4 booth.
articles.body:
For the second consecutive game of Dodgers vs. Braves, Fox will have a different play-by-play voice in the booth.

In Tuesday's Game 3 of the NLDS, it was Kenny Albert filling in alongside John Smoltz as L.A . took a 2-1 lead in the series.

Now, for Wednesday's Game 4, Braves fans will likely recognize another new voice in the booth filling in alongside Smoltz.

Here's why Fox's lead baseball announcer, Joe Davis, remains out for Game 4 of the Dodgers vs. Braves series.

Why Joe Davis remains sidelined for Dodgers-Braves NLDS Game 4

The Athletic's Andrew Marchand reported Tuesday that Davis is considered "day-to-day" with a sickness that caused him to lose his voice. At the time, he was set to miss Game 3 of the NLDS in the booth, with Albert taking his place.

Now, that illness is keeping Davis from calling Game 4 as well. Sports media reporter Richard Deitsch reported on Wednesday afternoon that Davis is "still under the weather," and in his place for Wednesday evening's game on play-by-play will be Brandon Gaudin.

Gaudin, like Davis is to the Dodgers, calls the Braves full-time in the regular season, but will now be on a national broadcast with Atlanta playing. Also known for his voice on the "Madden NFL" series since 2017, Gaudin has been the lead voice of the Braves since 2023.

It remains to be seen when Davis will be able to return to the booth alongside Smoltz, but with Fox carrying coverage of the NLCS soon, he will be assigned to that series if his health permits.
